title: Mastering Go Concurrency: Goroutines, Channels, and Select Patterns
description: A comprehensive SME-level course on building highly concurrent, lock-free, scalable backend systems in Go using worker pools, fan-out/fan-in pipelines, context cancellation, rate limiters, race detection, assessment quizzes, and interview prep.
body: Master Communicating Sequential Processes (CSP) in Go. This course covers everything from goroutine scheduler mechanics to production worker pools, rate limiters, context timeouts, data race elimination, assessment quizzes, and interview questions.

sections.title: Section 1: Concurrency Primitives & Go Scheduler Internal Architecture

lessons.title: Lesson 1.1: OS Threads vs. Go Scheduler M:N Model
lessons.body:
### The Scenario: Thread Starvation Crisis
Imagine running a backend service handling 50,000 concurrent HTTP requests. On traditional systems allocating 1MB OS thread stacks, 50,000 threads consume 50GB of RAM just for stack overhead, causing kernel thrashing and OS crash.

### Go's M:N Runtime Scheduler Solution
Go multiplexes N goroutines onto M operating system threads using P logical processors:
- **G (Goroutine):** Starts with an initial lightweight ~2KB resizable stack.
- **M (Machine):** OS kernel thread.
- **P (Processor):** Context resource managing runnable Goroutine queues (`GOMAXPROCS`).

```go
package main

import (
	"fmt"
	"runtime"
	"sync"
)

func main() {
	fmt.Printf("Logical CPUs (P): %d\n", runtime.NumCPU())
	var wg sync.WaitGroup
	for i := 0; i < 5; i++ {
		wg.Add(1)
		go func(id int) {
			defer wg.Done()
			fmt.Printf("Goroutine %d executing\n", id)
		}(i)
	}
	wg.Wait()
}
```

lessons.title: Lesson 1.2: Channel Memory Internals: Unbuffered vs. Buffered Channels
lessons.body:
### Unbuffered vs. Buffered Synchronization
- **Unbuffered Channels (`make(chan T)`):** Guarantee strict synchronization. Producer blocks until consumer is ready to receive.
- **Buffered Channels (`make(chan T, N)`):** Decouple producer and consumer execution up to buffer capacity N.

```go
package main

import "fmt"

func main() {
	ch := make(chan string, 2)
	ch <- "payload-1"
	ch <- "payload-2"
	
	fmt.Println(<-ch)
	fmt.Println(<-ch)
}
```

lessons.title: Lesson 3.1: Go Concurrency Assessment Quiz
lessons.body:
### Assessment Quiz: Go Concurrency Mechanics

#### Question 1: What happens if a goroutine attempts to write to an unbuffered channel when no receiver is ready?
- **A)** The channel drops the message silently.
- **B)** The sending goroutine blocks until a receiving goroutine reads from the channel.
- **C)** A runtime panic occurs (`panic: send on blocked channel`).
- **D)** The message is buffered dynamically in memory.

*Correct Answer:* **B**
*Explanation:* Unbuffered channels require synchronous handshake execution. Sending blocks until a reader is ready.

#### Question 2: What happens if a goroutine writes to a closed channel?
- **A)** The write succeeds silently.
- **B)** The channel returns `false`.
- **C)** A runtime panic occurs (`panic: send on closed channel`).
- **D)** The channel reopens automatically.

*Correct Answer:* **C**
*Explanation:* Writing to a closed channel causes an immediate runtime panic in Go.

lessons.title: Lesson 3.2: Senior Go Backend Technical Interview Prep
lessons.body:
### Technical Interview Q&A

#### Q1: How does Go handle goroutine memory allocation compared to Java or C++ threads?
**Model Answer:** Go starts goroutines with an initial lightweight ~2KB stack that resizes dynamically up to ~1GB, whereas Java/C++ OS threads allocate a fixed ~1MB-2MB stack upon creation. This enables Go applications to maintain hundreds of thousands of active goroutines on modest hardware.

#### Q2: Explain how `sync.WaitGroup` works and how to avoid deadlock when passing it to functions.
**Model Answer:** `sync.WaitGroup` tracks active goroutines using an atomic counter (`Add()`, `Done()`, `Wait()`). When passing a WaitGroup to a function or goroutine, you MUST pass it by pointer (`*sync.WaitGroup`); passing by value creates a copy, leaving the original WaitGroup counter unmodified and causing a permanent deadlock.
